contents.title: Singly Linked List
contents.definition: A singly linked list stores data in nodes where each node points to the next node in the sequence.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like a treasure hunt where each clue tells you only where the next clue is located.

contents.title: Traversing a Linked List
contents.definition: Traversing a linked list means starting at the head node and moving through each next pointer until the list ends.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like reading a chain of notes where each note tells you which note to open next.

contents.title: Print Linked List
contents.definition: Printing a linked list means visiting every node in order and displaying its stored data.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like calling out each stop one by one while moving through a route map.

contents.title: Count Nodes in Linked List
contents.definition: Counting nodes in a linked list means moving through the list and increasing a counter for each node visited.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like counting train coaches one by one from the engine to the last coach.

contents.title: Search in Linked List
contents.definition: Searching in a linked list compares each node value with the target until a match is found or the list ends.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like checking each name tag in a line until you find the person you want.

contents.title: FIND (Search in Linked List)
contents.definition: FIND is the textbook-style linked-list search procedure that returns the matching node location or reports failure.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like following a checklist procedure to inspect one box after another until the required item appears.

contents.title: Insert at Beginning of a Linked List
contents.definition: Insertion at the beginning creates a new node, links it to the current head, and updates the head pointer.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like placing a new coach at the front of a train so it becomes the first coach.

contents.title: Inserting After a Given Node in Linked List
contents.definition: This operation inserts a new node immediately after a known node by adjusting the next links carefully.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like inserting a new page into a notebook directly after a page you already opened.

contents.title: Inserting into a Sorted Linked List
contents.definition: Insertion into a sorted linked list finds the correct position first and then links the new node there.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like putting a new book into the right place on a shelf arranged by size.

contents.title: Deleting a Node from a Linked List (Given Location)
contents.definition: When the location is known, deletion relinks the previous node to the next node and removes the chosen node.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like removing one coach from the middle of a train and reconnecting the remaining coaches.

contents.title: Deleting a Node by ITEM in a Linked List
contents.definition: Deletion by item first searches for the required value and then removes the matching node safely.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like looking through a row of files for one label and removing that exact file when found.

contents.title: DELETE (Delete from Linked List)
contents.definition: DELETE is the textbook-style procedure for removing the first matching node from a linked list.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like following a written checklist to find the target record and remove it safely.

contents.title: Traversing a Circular Header List
contents.definition: Traversal in a circular header list starts after the header node and stops when the header node is reached again.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like moving around a circular track and knowing you are done when you return to the start marker.

contents.title: Searching a Circular Header List
contents.definition: Searching a circular header list checks nodes one by one and stops when the header node is reached again or the item is found.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like checking labels around a round display until you return to the starting label.

contents.title: Deleting from a Circular Header List
contents.definition: Deletion in a circular header list finds the matching node and reconnects the previous node so the circle remains valid.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like removing one bead from a closed necklace and joining the two loose ends again.
